about: What the public catalogue page (components.html) says about the story-component shelf, in plain words first (name, purpose, example, tags), beside what it reads from the engine's doc comments (the first sentence of each part's, shown in the For developers fold). One entry per root export whose doc comment carries @shelf, with an example of the same name in src/catalogue/examples; tests/shelfCatalogue.test.ts keeps the three together (O-080 T-335, plain words T-336).

jobs.switch: A switch: a button or choice that changes what is shown or where the camera looks
jobs.filter: A filter: lights some of the things in the scene and dims the rest
jobs.readout: A readout: a figure, key or picture that tells the visitor what they are looking at
jobs.explainer: An explainer: words that say what is going on

outOfTheBox.name: Title and About
outOfTheBox.text: Your title sits in the top bar. Pressing it opens an About panel with a status line, credits, links and the Built with Astraeus mark.

outOfTheBox.name: Picker and views
outOfTheBox.text: A choice in the bar between the things your page offers, and named views of one scene that show some objects and events and hide others.

outOfTheBox.name: Display switches
outOfTheBox.text: Orbit lines, labels, the Milky Way and the sky lines, each as a button in the bar or a row in a panel.

outOfTheBox.name: Timeline
outOfTheBox.text: Play and pause, a speed choice, a slider to scrub through time, and a list of the moments you add.

outOfTheBox.name: Camera and objects
outOfTheBox.text: A list of objects, buttons to focus on one or follow it, an overview, and, where you offer it, a view from out of a planet's sky.

outOfTheBox.name: Info cards
outOfTheBox.text: A card for each planet, path or group with its description, figures, source and known limits.

outOfTheBox.name: Story panels
outOfTheBox.text: Steps or moments with a title and some words, which can move the camera and pick out an object.

parts.name: Panel with a bar button
parts.purpose: A button in the top bar that opens a panel of your own, holding whatever you want to say or offer.
parts.example: a "Kirkwood gaps" button that opens a panel explaining the gaps in the asteroid belt.

uses.text: Put your story's own button in the bar; it opens a panel with the controls for that story.
Give a topic its own place, so the words are one press away and out of the way of the scene.

parts.name: Your own space
parts.purpose: An empty box inside a panel where you draw anything you like, such as a chart or a picture.
parts.example: a small chart of how fast a comet moves along its orbit, drawn inside a panel.

uses.text: Draw your own picture or chart in the panel; the viewer gives you an empty box and you fill it.
Any control the shelf does not have yet, until it does.

parts.name: Explainer text
parts.purpose: A heading, a few paragraphs and a small note, to say what the visitor is looking at.
parts.example: a short passage on why a planet speeds up near the Sun, with a note that the orbit is invented.

uses.text: Say what is on screen: a heading, a few paragraphs and a small note for a caveat or a source.
Change the words as the visitor moves the time or the camera.

parts.name: Action buttons
parts.purpose: A row of buttons that each do one thing, like flying the camera to a place you want the visitor to see.
parts.example: "Fly to the closest approach" and "Fly to the far end of the orbit" buttons for a guided tour.

uses.text: Buttons that fly the camera to a place the story wants the visitor to see.
A guided tour in a panel: one button for each stop.

parts.name: Filter chips
parts.purpose: Small toggle buttons for picking one group or several; your story decides what changes, such as lighting that group up.
parts.example: chips for "Rocky", "Icy" and "Metal" asteroids, so the visitor can see one kind at a time.

uses.text: Pick one group, or several, to light up while the rest dims.
A choice between a few modes of the same scene, shown as chips instead of a menu.

parts.name: Colour key
parts.purpose: A key that says what each colour means and how many things wear it.
parts.example: a key beside the chips showing that blue is icy, orange is rocky, with a count for each.

uses.text: Say what each colour means, with how many things wear it.
Sit beside a set of chips so the visitor can see what each chip lights.
